system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-12-08 00:00:00 to 2186-12-10 20:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old man with recurrent primary central nervous system lymphoma was admitted for his 25th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy as part of reinduction therapy. He presented electively in stable condition and received methotrexate 8 g/m² with urinary alkalinization. Temozolomide 240 mg daily was continued on a 7-day on/7-day off cycle. Leucovorin rescue was initiated 24 hours post-infusion. Methotrexate levels declined appropriately to 0.17, and he tolerated treatment without complications. Sodium remained stable, and no adjustments were needed to desmopressin. He reported increased depressive symptoms, prompting a psychiatry clinic referral. He was discharged home with instructions to continue leucovorin and bicarbonate for 24 hours, resume all home medications, and follow up for Rituxan and MRI surveillance in one month.
problems: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Other malignant lymphomas, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Essential and other specified forms of tremor

conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of your hospitalists. You're here today for your 26th cycle of high-dose methotrexate. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’m doing okay—no fevers, no nausea. Just ready to get this infusion done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We’ll start with some baseline labs and vitals. You’ve been on this regimen for a while, so we know the drill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s routine by now. But I did want to mention—I’ve been feeling a bit down lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see in your chart you saw your psychiatrist recently. You stopped Zoloft and tried Remeron, but it caused nightmares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The nightmares were bad. I stopped it. My mood’s not terrible, but it’s not great either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The inpatient psychiatry team reviewed your case. There’s a plan to switch your seizure medication from Keppra to Depakote at your next visit—it might help your mood too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that. Is that safe with my lymphoma treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. Depakote is often used for both seizures and mood stabilization. We’ll coordinate with your neurologist. But since you’re being discharged soon, you’ll start it at your next clinic visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. White count is a bit low at 3.4, but that’s expected with chemotherapy. Potassium is 3.7, so we’ll give you some oral supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? The low potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this level. It’s mild and common with IV fluids. We’ll replace it orally, and it should stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my sodium? I remember last time it dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sodium is 135—perfect. No signs of hyponatremia. We held your desmopressin this morning just to be safe, but you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, right. Because of the fluid overload risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re giving a lot of IV fluid with the methotrexate, so we have to balance that with your diabetes insipidus treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your methotrexate infusion now—19,680 mg over several hours. The nurse will monitor your urine pH to keep it alkaline, which helps clear the drug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin starts tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 24 hours after the infusion ends. It protects your healthy cells from methotrexate. We’ll check your methotrexate level every morning until it’s low enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You did well—no nausea, no reactions. We’ll keep an eye on your labs overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I’m feeling tired, but that’s normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level is 0.37—coming down as expected. Liver enzymes are slightly up, but that’s typical and temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any concern about my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. We monitor it closely. It usually recovers on its own after chemo. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my facial numbness? Still there, but not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We still think it’s related to seizure activity. Keppra is helping some. You’ll follow up with Dr. Lee for an EEG soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, next week. I’ve been using medical marijuana at night—helps me relax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just make sure it doesn’t interact with your other meds. We have you listed for cannabis use in your chart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is 102/62—lower than usual. You’re on lisinopril for hypertension. Should we adjust it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit lightheaded. Maybe it’s too much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold it today and check again tomorrow. It could be from the fluids or the chemo. We’ll play it safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your methotrexate level is now 0.17. That means you can stop leucovorin and bicarbonate after today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m good to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve tolerated everything well. No infections, no hyponatremia, no complications. We’ll discharge you this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? Do I restart everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume all your home medications, including desmopressin, lisinopril, Keppra, and temozolomide. Continue the Depakote plan with your neurologist at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up for MRI and Rituxan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same as before—Rituxan in three weeks, MRI surveillance in a month. Call us if you develop fever, confusion, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I worry about TB? With the chemo and my history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. You’re at higher risk, but your tests were negative, and we’ve been monitoring. Just stay alert for cough, fever, or weight loss—and report them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your discharge papers shortly. Nurse will go over the instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the medical marijuana responsibly—just know it’s not a substitute for your prescribed treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. It’s just for sleep and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fair enough. Just keep your team informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll sign the discharge order. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old man with recurrent primary central nervous system lymphoma was admitted for his 26th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. He presented electively in stable condition and received methotrexate 8 g/m² with urinary alkalinization. Temozolomide was continued on a 7-day on/7-day off cycle. Leucovorin rescue was initiated 24 hours post-infusion, and methotrexate levels declined appropriately to 0.17. He tolerated treatment without complications. Hyponatremia did not develop, and potassium was managed with oral supplementation. Blood pressure was lower than baseline, prompting temporary hold of lisinopril. The patient reported persistent mild depressive symptoms; a plan to switch from Keppra to Depakote for potential mood benefit was discussed but deferred to outpatient follow-up. He was discharged home with instructions to resume all home medications and continue follow-up for Rituxan and MRI surveillance.
